content_html:
Emptiness and the Role of Memory

If everything is empty of inherent existence, what role does memory have?

Under śūnyatā (emptiness), nothing has fixed essence; things arise dependently. Memory still matters—conventionally. It is a dependently-arisen process that preserves functional continuity, guides prediction and action, and supports ethical cultivation. Because it is empty, memory is plastic: it is reconstructed, context-bound, and revisable, which is precisely why it can liberate (when used wisely) or mislead (when reified).

In the Madhyamaka tradition, emptiness means lack of intrinsic essence and dependent origination. Nāgārjuna frames this via the “two truths”: conventional (everyday functioning, language, practices) and ultimate (emptiness of inherent existence). On this view, memory has no self-subsisting core, but conventionally it exists and does work in the world.

  • Two truths: conventional vs. ultimate; failure to understand both misses the Buddha’s teaching
  • Dependence: all phenomena—including mental events like recollection—arise from causes, conditions, and conceptual imputation.

What Memory Does (Conventional Role)

Philosophically, memory grounds personal continuity, knowledge of the past, and social coordination. Practically, it allows learning, skill, planning, and responsibility. But these functions do not require a metaphysical essence—only reliable, dependently-arisen processes.

Think of memory as a working interface: patterns that persist just enough to coordinate action, yet remain open to update.

Contemporary cognitive science portrays episodic remembering as constructive: the brain recombines fragments to rebuild the past and simulate futures. Retrieval reopens a labile window (reconsolidation), so traces are updated. In predictive-processing terms, memory supplies priors for minimizing surprise; uncertainty (not-knowing) is part of how models adapt. Emptiness here shows up as flexibility.

  • Ontologically: Memory is empty — no essence, only dependence.
  • Functionally: It scaffolds prediction, coordination, and identity (conventional truth).
  • Ethically: As sati, memory guides right action and the gradual dissolution of reification.
  • Practically: Treat memories as hypotheses: useful, revisable, to be tested against present causes and effects.

Buddhist Psychology (Continuity without Essence)

Classical Abhidharma explains continuity via momentary mental events in streams (santāna), while Yogācāra models continuity with a “storehouse” consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) that carries seeds (bīja)—habituations shaping future cognition. Madhyamaka remains agnostic about such posits at the ultimate level, yet allows them as conventional heuristics. Across these schools, memory’s job is to coordinate experience without reifying a self or a static past.

In early Buddhist sources, sati (mindfulness) retains a core sense of remembering—keeping the object in mind and recalling what is wholesome and skillful. Memory, as recollection, stabilizes attention and orients action, supporting insight into impermanence and emptiness. Thus, memory is both tool and training ground for non-clinging.
